questions.question_text: Ravi's income rises by 20% and his expenditure rises by 10%. As a result, his savings rise by 50%. What percentage of his original income did he originally save?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Let income = 100 and expenditure = E. New savings: 120 − 1.1E = 1.5(100 − E) ⇒ 0.4E = 30 ⇒ E = 75. Savings = 25% of income.

questions.question_text: In a two-candidate election, 10% of registered voters did not vote and 10% of the votes cast were invalid. The winner got 54% of the valid votes and won by 1,620 votes. How many registered voters were there?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Valid votes = 0.9 × 0.9 × N = 0.81N. The margin is 54% − 46% = 8% of valid votes: 0.08 × 0.81N = 0.0648N = 1620 ⇒ N = 25,000.

questions.question_text: A train passes a man walking at 3 km/h in the same direction in 10 seconds, and a man walking at 6 km/h towards it in 8 seconds. What is the length of the train?

A and B start together from the same point on a 1,200 m circular track and run in the same direction at 5 m/s and 7 m/s. After how many seconds will they first be together at the starting point again?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: A completes a lap every 240 s and B every 1200/7 s. Both are at the start at times that are multiples of both: 240a = 1200b/7 ⇒ 7a = 5b, smallest a = 5 ⇒ 1,200 s. (They do meet at 600 s too, but halfway round the track, not at the start.)

questions.question_text: A boat goes 30 km upstream and 44 km downstream in 10 hours. It goes 40 km upstream and 55 km downstream in 13 hours. What is the speed of the stream?

options.B: 3 km/h
options.C: 4 km/h

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Let u = 1/upstream speed and d = 1/downstream speed: 30u + 44d = 10 and 40u + 55d = 13. Solving gives u = 1/5 and d = 1/11, so the upstream speed is 5 and the downstream speed 11. Stream = (11 − 5)/2 = 3 km/h.

questions.question_text: Walking at 5 km/h, Meera reaches office 6 minutes late. Walking at 6 km/h, she reaches 4 minutes early. How far is her office?

options.B: 5 km
options.C: 6 km

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The time difference is 10 min = 1/6 h. d/5 − d/6 = 1/6 ⇒ d/30 = 1/6 ⇒ d = 5 km.

questions.question_text: 12 men or 18 women can finish a piece of work in 14 days. How many days will 8 men and 16 women take to finish it?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 1 man = 18/12 = 1.5 women. 8 men + 16 women = 28 women. Work = 18 × 14 = 252 woman-days ⇒ 252/28 = 9 days.

questions.question_text: Pipes A and B fill a tank in 20 and 30 minutes respectively, and pipe C empties it in 15 minutes. All three are opened on an empty tank, and C is closed after 10 minutes. How many minutes in total does it take to fill the tank?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: With all three open: 1/20 + 1/30 − 1/15 = 1/60 per minute, so 10 minutes fill 1/6. The remaining 5/6 at A + B = 1/12 per minute takes 10 minutes. Total = 20 minutes.

questions.question_text: A is twice as efficient as B, and together they finish a job in 14 days. How many days would A alone take?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: If B does b per day, A does 2b, so 3b = 1/14 ⇒ b = 1/42 and A = 1/21 ⇒ 21 days.

questions.question_text: A vessel contains 80 litres of pure wine. 8 litres are taken out and replaced with water, and this is done three times in all. How much wine is left?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Each operation keeps 72/80 = 0.9 of the wine. Wine left = 80 × 0.9³ = 58.32 L.

questions.question_text: Alloy X has copper and zinc in the ratio 3 : 2, and alloy Y has them in the ratio 1 : 3. In what ratio (X : Y) must they be mixed to get an alloy with equal amounts of copper and zinc?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Copper fraction: X = 0.6, Y = 0.25, target 0.5. By alligation, X : Y = (0.5 − 0.25) : (0.6 − 0.5) = 0.25 : 0.1 = 5 : 2.

questions.question_text: A sum grows to ₹13,310 in 3 years and to ₹14,641 in 4 years at compound interest (compounded annually). What is the principal?
The difference between compound and simple interest on a sum for 3 years at 10% per annum is ₹93. What is the sum?
The present ages of A and B are in the ratio 5 : 7. Six years ago they were in the ratio 2 : 3. What is the sum of their present ages?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: (5k − 6)/(7k − 6) = 2/3 ⇒ 15k − 18 = 14k − 12 ⇒ k = 6. The ages are 30 and 42, so the sum is 72.

questions.question_text: A bag has ₹1, 50-paise and 25-paise coins in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4 by number, worth ₹216 in total. How many 50-paise coins are there?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Value per set of (2, 3, 4) coins = 2 + 1.5 + 1 = ₹4.5. Sets = 216/4.5 = 48. 50-paise coins = 3 × 48 = 144.

questions.question_text: The roots of x² − px + 12 = 0 differ by 1, and p > 0. What is p?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: (r₁ − r₂)² = (r₁ + r₂)² − 4r₁r₂ = p² − 48 = 1 ⇒ p = 7. (The roots are 3 and 4.)

questions.question_text: If α and β are the roots of x² − 5x + 3 = 0, what is α³ + β³?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: α + β = 5 and αβ = 3. α³ + β³ = (α + β)³ − 3αβ(α + β) = 125 − 45 = 80.

questions.question_text: The digits of a two-digit number add up to 9. Reversing the digits increases the number by 27. What is the number?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Let the number be 10a + b with a + b = 9. Reversing adds 9(b − a) = 27 ⇒ b − a = 3. So a = 3, b = 6, and the number is 36.

questions.question_text: For which values of x is x² − 7x + 10 < 0?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: x² − 7x + 10 = (x − 2)(x − 5) is negative strictly between its roots, so 2 < x < 5.

questions.question_text: What is the minimum value of (x² + 2x + 9)/(x + 1) for x > −1?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: (x² + 2x + 9)/(x + 1) = (x + 1) + 8/(x + 1). By AM–GM this is at least 2√8 = 4√2, with equality when x + 1 = 2√2.

questions.question_text: f(x) + 2f(1/x) = 3x for every non-zero real x. What is f(2)?
What is the minimum value of f(x) = |x − 2| + |x − 5|?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The sum of distances from x to 2 and to 5 is smallest (= 5 − 2 = 3) for any x between 2 and 5.

questions.question_text: If log₂(log₃(log₂ x)) = 1, what is x?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: log₃(log₂ x) = 2 ⇒ log₂ x = 9 ⇒ x = 2⁹ = 512.

questions.question_text: Solve log₂(x − 1) + log₂(x + 1) = 3.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: log₂[(x − 1)(x + 1)] = 3 ⇒ x² − 1 = 8 ⇒ x = ±3. But x − 1 > 0 is needed for the log, so only x = 3 works.

questions.question_text: What is the sum of all positive divisors of 72?
What is the highest power of 3 that divides 100!?
What is the smallest number that leaves remainder 3 when divided by 5, 6 or 8, and is divisible by 9?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Such numbers are 120k + 3. We need 120k + 3 ≡ 0 (mod 9). 120 ≡ 3, so 3k + 3 ≡ 0 (mod 9) ⇒ k ≡ 2 (mod 3). Smallest k = 2 ⇒ 243.

questions.question_text: What are the last two digits of 3⁴⁰?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 3²⁰ ≡ 1 (mod 100) (Carmichael's λ(100) = 20; check 3¹⁰ = 59049 ≡ 49 and 49² = 2401 ≡ 01). So 3⁴⁰ ≡ 1 ⇒ last two digits 01.

questions.question_text: In triangle ABC, AB = AC = 13 cm and BC = 10 cm. What is the inradius?

options.C: 4 cm

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The height to BC is √(13² − 5²) = 12, so area = 60. s = (13 + 13 + 10)/2 = 18. r = Area/s = 60/18 = 10/3 cm.

questions.question_text: From a point P 13 cm from the centre O of a circle of radius 5 cm, tangents PA and PB are drawn. What is the area of quadrilateral OAPB?

options.B: 60 cm²
options.C: 65 cm²

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Tangent length = √(13² − 5²) = 12. OAPB is two right triangles, each (1/2) × 5 × 12 = 30, so the area is 60 cm².

questions.question_text: What is the area of a regular hexagon with side 6 cm?

options.B: 54√3 cm²
options.C: 72√3 cm²

questions.pedagogical_explanation: A regular hexagon is 6 equilateral triangles: 6 × (√3/4) × 36 = 54√3 cm².

questions.question_text: A triangle has vertices (0, 0), (6, 0) and (0, 8). What is the distance between its circumcentre and its incentre?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: It's right-angled at the origin, so the circumcentre is the hypotenuse midpoint (3, 4) and R = 5. Inradius r = (6 + 8 − 10)/2 = 2, so the incentre is (2, 2). Distance = √(1² + 2²) = √5. (Check: Euler's OI² = R² − 2Rr = 25 − 20 = 5.)

questions.question_text: A 12 × 8 × 6 cm cuboid is painted on all faces and cut into 1 cm cubes. How many cubes have no painted face?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The unpainted cubes form the inner block (12 − 2) × (8 − 2) × (6 − 2) = 10 × 6 × 4 = 240.

questions.question_text: The space diagonal of a cube is 6√3 cm. What is its total surface area?

options.B: 144 cm²
options.C: 216 cm²

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Diagonal = a√3 ⇒ a = 6. TSA = 6a² = 216 cm².

questions.question_text: How many rectangles (including squares) are there on an 8 × 8 chessboard?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Pick 2 of the 9 horizontal lines and 2 of the 9 vertical lines: C(9, 2)² = 36² = 1,296. (204 is the number of squares.)

questions.question_text: How many four-digit numbers have digits that strictly increase from left to right (e.g. 1357)?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 0 can't appear (it would have to come first). Any 4 distinct digits from 1–9 can be arranged in increasing order in exactly one way: C(9, 4) = 126.

questions.question_text: Three fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum is 10?
Two cards are drawn at random from a standard 52-card deck. What is the probability that both are aces or both are kings?
A and B take turns tossing a fair coin, A first. The first to get a head wins. What is the probability that A wins?
The 5th term of an AP is 17 and the 12th term is 38. What is the 20th term?
An infinite GP has first term 4 and sum 12. What is the sum of its first three terms?
The price of a gadget is first raised by 25% and then reduced by x%, so that the final price is 10% above the original price. What is x?
A shopkeeper allows successive discounts of 20% and 10% on the marked price and still earns a profit of 8% on cost price. By what percentage is the marked price above the cost price?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Selling price = 0.8 × 0.9 × MP = 0.72 MP = 1.08 CP. So MP = 1.5 CP, i.e. 50% above cost.

questions.question_text: A can finish a job in 12 days and B in 18 days. They work together for 4 days, after which A leaves. In how many days in all is the job completed?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: In 4 days together: 4 × (1/12 + 1/18) = 4 × 5/36 = 5/9 of the work. The remaining 4/9 is done by B at 1/18 per day, which takes 8 days. Total = 4 + 8 = 12 days.

questions.question_text: What is the remainder when 2^100 is divided by 7?
The roots of x² − 7x + k = 0 differ by 3. What is the value of k?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Let the roots be a and a + 3. Sum = 2a + 3 = 7, so a = 2. The roots are 2 and 5, so k = product = 10.

questions.question_text: The sides of a triangle are 13 cm, 14 cm and 15 cm. What is the radius of its incircle?

options.B: 3.5 cm
options.C: 4 cm

questions.question_text: A chord of length 24 cm is at a distance of 5 cm from the centre of a circle. What is the radius of the circle?

options.B: 13 cm
options.C: 14 cm

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Half-chord = 12. Radius² = 12² + 5² = 169, so r = 13 cm.

questions.question_text: In how many ways can the letters of the word BANANA be arranged so that no two A's are adjacent?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Arrange B, N, N first: 3!/2! = 3 ways. This creates 4 gaps; choose 3 of them for the A's: C(4,3) = 4. Total = 3 × 4 = 12.

questions.question_text: Two fair dice are thrown. What is the probability that the sum of the numbers is a prime number?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Prime sums: 2 (1 way), 3 (2), 5 (4), 7 (6), 11 (2) = 15 favourable outcomes out of 36. Probability = 15/36 = 5/12.

questions.question_text: If log₂ x + log₄ x = 6, what is x?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: log₄ x = (1/2) log₂ x, so (3/2) log₂ x = 6, giving log₂ x = 4 and x = 16.

questions.question_text: Two varieties of rice costing ₹40/kg and ₹55/kg are mixed and the mixture is sold at ₹54/kg at a profit of 20%. In what ratio were the cheaper and dearer varieties mixed?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Cost price of the mixture = 54/1.2 = ₹45. By alligation, cheaper : dearer = (55 − 45) : (45 − 40) = 10 : 5 = 2 : 1.

questions.question_text: Pipe A fills a tank in 20 minutes, pipe B in 30 minutes, and pipe C empties it in 60 minutes. If all three are opened together, in how many minutes is the empty tank filled?
In a class of 60 students, 35 play cricket, 30 play football and 10 play neither. How many students play both games?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Students playing at least one game = 60 − 10 = 50. Both = 35 + 30 − 50 = 15.

questions.question_text: The price of sugar rises by 25%. By what percentage must a family cut its sugar consumption so that its spending on sugar stays the same?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: New price = 1.25 × old. To keep spending equal, consumption must become 1/1.25 = 0.8 of the old, a cut of 20%.

questions.question_text: A shopkeeper sells two phones for ₹1,200 each, making a 20% profit on one and a 20% loss on the other. What is his overall result?

options.B: Loss of ₹100
options.C: Loss of ₹48

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Cost prices are 1200/1.2 = ₹1,000 and 1200/0.8 = ₹1,500. Total cost ₹2,500, total revenue ₹2,400, so a loss of ₹100.

questions.question_text: Walking at 5 km/h, Meena reaches her office 6 minutes late. Walking at 6 km/h, she reaches 4 minutes early. How far is her office?

options.B: 4 km
options.C: 5 km

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The two times differ by 6 + 4 = 10 minutes = 1/6 h. So d/5 − d/6 = d/30 = 1/6, giving d = 5 km.

questions.question_text: Two trains, 150 m and 100 m long, run on parallel tracks in opposite directions at 54 km/h and 36 km/h. How long do they take to cross each other completely?

options.B: 25 seconds
options.C: 50 seconds

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Relative speed = 90 km/h = 25 m/s. Distance to cover = 150 + 100 = 250 m. Time = 250/25 = 10 s.

questions.question_text: 6 men or 9 women can finish a job in 12 days. In how many days will 4 men and 6 women together finish it?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 6 men = 9 women, so 1 man = 1.5 women. The job is 9 × 12 = 108 woman-days. 4 men + 6 women = 6 + 6 = 12 women, so 108/12 = 9 days.

questions.question_text: ₹2,100 is divided among A, B and C such that A : B = 2 : 3 and B : C = 4 : 5. What is C's share?
Ravi spends 75% of his income. His income rises by 20% and his spending rises by 10%. By what percentage do his savings increase?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Take income 100: spending 75, savings 25. New income 120, new spending 82.5, new savings 37.5. Increase = 12.5/25 = 50%.

questions.question_text: A function satisfies f(x) + 2f(1/x) = 3x for every x ≠ 0. What is f(2)?
Given log₁₀2 = 0.301, how many digits does 2^50 have?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: log₁₀(2^50) = 50 × 0.301 = 15.05. A number whose log lies between 15 and 16 has 15 + 1 = 16 digits.

questions.question_text: In a geometric progression with real terms, the 3rd term is 12 and the 6th term is 96. What is the sum of the first 5 terms?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: r³ = 96/12 = 8, so r = 2 and the first term is 12/4 = 3. Sum = 3(2⁵ − 1)/(2 − 1) = 93.

questions.question_text: How many ordered pairs of positive integers (x, y) satisfy 3x + 5y = 100?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 100 − 5y must be a positive multiple of 3. 5y ≡ 1 (mod 3) means y ≡ 2 (mod 3): y = 2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17 (y = 20 gives x = 0). That is 6 pairs.

questions.question_text: A right triangle has legs 6 cm and 8 cm. What is the length of the altitude drawn to the hypotenuse?

options.B: 4.5 cm
options.C: 5.2 cm

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Hypotenuse = 10. Twice the area = 6 × 8 = 10 × h, so h = 4.8 cm.

questions.question_text: Two circles of radii 7 cm and 1 cm have their centres 10 cm apart. What is the length of a direct (outer) common tangent?

options.B: 6 cm
options.C: 4√6 cm

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Direct common tangent = √(d² − (r₁ − r₂)²) = √(100 − 36) = 8 cm. (The trap is 6 cm, which uses r₁ + r₂: that is the transverse common tangent, √(100 − 64) = 6.)

questions.question_text: Each interior angle of a regular polygon is 150°. How many diagonals does it have?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Each exterior angle is 30°, so there are 360/30 = 12 sides. Diagonals = 12 × 9/2 = 54.

questions.question_text: What are the last two digits of 7^42?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 7⁴ = 2401 ends in 01, so 7⁴⁰ = (7⁴)¹⁰ also ends in 01. Then 7⁴² ends like 01 × 49 = 49.

questions.question_text: A committee of 4 is to be chosen from 5 men and 4 women so that it has at least 2 women. In how many ways can this be done?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 2 women: C(4,2) × C(5,2) = 60. 3 women: C(4,3) × 5 = 20. 4 women: 1. Total = 81. (126 is all committees, with no condition.)

questions.question_text: A number is picked at random from 1 to 50. What is the probability that it is divisible by 3 or by 5?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Multiples of 3: 16, of 5: 10, of both (15): 3. By inclusion–exclusion, 16 + 10 − 3 = 23, so 23/50.

questions.question_text: A trader claims to sell rice at 10% above cost price, but his weighing scale shows 1 kg when only 800 g is on it. What is his actual profit percentage?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Take the cost of 1 kg as ₹100. The customer pays ₹110 but receives 800 g, which cost the trader ₹80. Profit = 30/80 = 37.5%.

questions.question_text: In a 1 km race, A beats B by 100 m, and B beats C by 100 m. By how many metres does A beat C in a 1 km race?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: When A runs 1000 m, B runs 900 m. When B runs 1000 m, C runs 900 m, so when B runs 900 m, C runs 810 m. A beats C by 1000 − 810 = 190 m. (Adding 100 + 100 is the trap.)

questions.question_text: A and B together can finish a job in 12 days. A works alone for 6 days, and then B alone finishes the remaining work in 16 days. In how many days can A alone finish the whole job?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Let A's daily rate be a. Then B's rate is 1/12 − a, and 6a + 16(1/12 − a) = 1. So 4/3 − 10a = 1, giving a = 1/30. A alone needs 30 days.

questions.question_text: A sum of money at compound interest (compounded annually) amounts to ₹8,820 in 2 years and ₹9,261 in 3 years. What is the sum?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: One year's growth: 9261 / 8820 = 1.05, so the rate is 5%. Principal = 8820 / 1.05² = 8820 / 1.1025 = ₹8,000.

questions.question_text: What is the minimum value of |x − 1| + |x − 4| + |x − 9| over all real x?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: A sum of distances from points is smallest at the median point, x = 4: 3 + 0 + 5 = 8.

questions.question_text: If log_a b = 2 and log_b c = 3, what is log_ac b?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: b = a² and c = b³ = a⁶, so ac = a⁷. Then log_ac b = log(a²)/log(a⁷) = 2/7.

questions.question_text: x and y are positive real numbers with x + y = 10. What is the maximum value of x²y?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Write 10 = x/2 + x/2 + y. By AM ≥ GM, (x/2)(x/2)(y) ≤ (10/3)³, so x²y ≤ 4 × 1000/27 = 4000/27, reached at x = 20/3, y = 10/3. (2000/9 is larger, but it cannot be reached.)

questions.question_text: The HCF of two numbers is 12 and their LCM is 720. How many such pairs of numbers exist? (Treat (a, b) and (b, a) as the same pair.)
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Write the numbers as 12m and 12n with m, n co-prime and mn = 720/12 = 60 = 2² × 3 × 5. Each of the three prime powers goes wholly to m or to n: 2³ = 8 ordered ways, so 4 unordered pairs: (12, 720), (36, 240), (48, 180), (60, 144).

questions.question_text: In triangle ABC, AB = 10 cm and AC = 14 cm. The bisector of angle A meets BC at D, and BD = 5 cm. What is the length of AD?

options.C: 11 cm

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Angle bisector theorem: BD/DC = AB/AC = 10/14, so DC = 7. Bisector length: AD² = AB × AC − BD × DC = 140 − 35 = 105, so AD = √105 cm.

questions.question_text: A right circular cone of height 30 cm is cut by a plane parallel to its base, at a height of 10 cm above the base. What is the ratio of the volume of the small cone (on top) to the volume of the frustum?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The small cone has height 20, so it is similar to the full cone with ratio 2/3. Volumes scale as the cube: small = 8/27 of the whole, so the frustum = 19/27. Ratio = 8 : 19. (8 : 27 compares with the whole cone, not the frustum.)

questions.question_text: A bag has 5 red and 4 blue balls. Three balls are drawn together at random. What is the probability that the three balls include both colours?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Total ways = C(9, 3) = 84. All red: C(5, 3) = 10; all blue: C(4, 3) = 4. Probability = 1 − 14/84 = 70/84 = 5/6.

questions.question_text: In a survey of 100 people, 80 like tea, 75 like coffee and 70 like juice. What is the minimum number of people who like all three?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: People who do not like tea, coffee and juice number 20, 25 and 30. Even if these groups do not overlap, at most 75 people miss at least one drink. So at least 100 − 75 = 25 like all three.

questions.question_text: A shop runs a "buy 3, get 1 free" offer and still makes a profit of 20%. By what percentage is the marked price above the cost price?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Take the cost of one item as 100. The customer pays for 3 and takes 4, so 3 × MP = 1.2 × 400 = 480, giving MP = 160. The marked price is 60% above cost.

questions.question_text: A and B start together from the same point on a circular track of length 600 m and run in opposite directions at 15 m/s and 25 m/s. If they keep running, at how many distinct points on the track will they meet?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Their speeds are in the ratio 3 : 5. Running in opposite directions, they meet at (3 + 5) = 8 distinct points. Check: relative speed 40 m/s, so they meet every 15 s; A covers 225 m between meetings, and 225 × 8 = 1800 = 3 laps, so the pattern repeats after 8 meetings.

questions.question_text: A and B start a business with ₹40,000 and ₹60,000. After 4 months, A adds ₹20,000 and B withdraws ₹10,000. The profit at the end of the year is ₹55,000. What is A's share?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: A: 40,000 × 4 + 60,000 × 8 = 6,40,000 rupee-months. B: 60,000 × 4 + 50,000 × 8 = 6,40,000. The shares are equal, so A gets ₹27,500. (Using only the starting amounts gives ₹22,000, the trap.)

questions.question_text: How many times in a day (24 hours) are the hour hand and the minute hand of a clock at right angles?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The minute hand gains 330° on the hour hand every hour, so in 12 hours it gains 11 full rounds and passes each right-angle position (90° and 270°) 11 times: 22 times in 12 hours, 44 in a day. (48 assumes two right angles in every hour, but the ones at exactly 3:00 and 9:00 each serve two neighbouring hours, so 2 are lost in every 12 hours.)

questions.question_text: If f(x) = (x − 1)/(x + 1), what is f(f(f(f(f(3)))))?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: f(3) = 1/2, f(1/2) = −1/3, f(−1/3) = −2, f(−2) = 3. The values repeat every 4 steps, so the fifth application gives f(3) = 1/2.

questions.question_text: If 2^x = 3^y = 6^z (with x, y, z non-zero), which of these is true?

options.B: z = (x + y)/xy
options.C: z = x + y

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Let the common value be k. Then x = log k / log 2, y = log k / log 3, z = log k / log 6. So 1/x + 1/y = (log 2 + log 3)/log k = log 6/log k = 1/z, which gives z = xy/(x + y).

questions.question_text: When a polynomial p(x) is divided by (x − 1) the remainder is 3, and when divided by (x − 2) the remainder is 5. What is the remainder when p(x) is divided by (x − 1)(x − 2)?

options.C: 3x

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The remainder has the form ax + b. From the remainder theorem: a + b = 3 and 2a + b = 5, so a = 2, b = 1. Remainder = 2x + 1.

questions.question_text: Real numbers x and y satisfy x² + y² = 25. What is the maximum value of 3x + 4y?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, (3x + 4y)² ≤ (3² + 4²)(x² + y²) = 25 × 25, so 3x + 4y ≤ 25, reached at x = 3, y = 4. (35 would need x = y = 5, which is not on the circle.)

questions.question_text: An equilateral triangle is inscribed in a circle of radius 6 cm. What is the area of the part of the circle that lies outside the triangle?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Side of the triangle = R√3 = 6√3. Area of triangle = (√3/4)(6√3)² = 27√3. Circle = 36π. Required area = 36π − 27√3 sq cm.

questions.question_text: The line 3x + 4y = 24 forms a triangle with the coordinate axes. What is the distance of the incentre of this triangle from the origin?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The triangle has legs 8 and 6 and hypotenuse 10. For a right triangle, inradius = (6 + 8 − 10)/2 = 2, and the incentre is (2, 2). Distance from origin = 2√2.

questions.question_text: In how many ways can 5 boys and 5 girls sit around a round table so that no two boys sit next to each other?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Seat the girls first around the table: (5 − 1)! = 24 ways. This leaves 5 gaps, one between each pair of girls, for the 5 boys: 5! = 120 ways. Total = 24 × 120 = 2880.

questions.question_text: A family has two children. You are told that at least one of them is a boy. What is the probability that both are boys? (Assume each child is equally likely to be a boy or a girl.)
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The equally likely cases are BB, BG, GB, GG. "At least one boy" leaves BB, BG, GB. Only BB has two boys, so the probability is 1/3. (1/2 is the common trap.)

questions.question_text: Two different numbers are chosen at random from 1 to 20. What is the probability that their sum is even?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The sum is even when both are even or both are odd: C(10,2) + C(10,2) = 45 + 45 = 90. Total = C(20,2) = 190. Probability = 90/190 = 9/19. (It is not 1/2 because the two numbers must be different.)

questions.question_text: A and B together can finish a job in 12 days. They work together for 4 days, after which A leaves and B finishes the rest in 20 more days. Had C, who is twice as efficient as B, joined A and B from the start, how many days would the whole job have taken?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: A + B do 1/12 per day, so in 4 days they finish 1/3. B does the remaining 2/3 in 20 days, so B alone takes 30 days and C does 1/15 per day. Then A + B + C do 1/12 + 1/15 = 9/60 = 3/20 per day, and the job takes 20/3 days ≈ 6.67 days.

questions.question_text: The difference between the compound interest (compounded annually) and the simple interest on a sum for 3 years at 10% per annum is ₹930. What is the sum, in ₹?
The average of a list of numbers is 36. When one number, 60, is removed, the average of the remaining numbers becomes 34.5. How many numbers were in the original list?
A boat makes a round trip of 84 km upstream and 84 km back downstream in 10 hours. The upstream leg takes 4 hours more than the downstream leg. What is the speed of the boat in still water, in km/h?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Downstream takes 3 h and upstream 7 h. So b + s = 28 and b − s = 12, giving b = 20 km/h.

questions.question_text: If log₂x + log₄x + log₁₆x = 7, what is the value of x?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Writing everything in base 2: log₂x (1 + 1/2 + 1/4) = 7, so (7/4) log₂x = 7, giving log₂x = 4 and x = 16.

questions.question_text: A function f satisfies f(x) + 2f(1 − x) = x² for every real x. What is f(3)?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Put x = 3: f(3) + 2f(−2) = 9. Put x = −2: f(−2) + 2f(3) = 4. Doubling the second and subtracting the first: 3f(3) = 8 − 9 = −1, so f(3) = −1/3.

questions.question_text: How many ordered pairs of integers (x, y) satisfy |x| + 2|y| ≤ 6?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: For each y with |y| ≤ 3, x ranges over |x| ≤ 6 − 2|y|, giving 2(6 − 2|y|) + 1 values: y = 0 gives 13; |y| = 1 gives 9 (twice); |y| = 2 gives 5 (twice); |y| = 3 gives 1 (twice). Total 13 + 18 + 10 + 2 = 43.

questions.question_text: x and y are non-negative real numbers with x + y = 10. What is the maximum possible value of x²y? (Give the answer as a fraction or decimal if needed.)
A right triangle has legs of length 20 and 21. What is the product of its inradius and circumradius?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The hypotenuse is √(400 + 441) = 29. Inradius = (20 + 21 − 29)/2 = 6, circumradius = 29/2. Product = 87.

questions.question_text: Two parallel chords of a circle of radius 13 cm lie on the same side of the centre. One chord is 24 cm long and the distance between the chords is 7 cm. What is the length of the other chord, in cm?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The 24 cm chord is √(169 − 144) = 5 cm from the centre. The other is 12 cm from the centre (same side, 7 cm further), so its half-length is √(169 − 144) = 5 and its length 10 cm.

questions.question_text: What is the area of the quadrilateral with vertices (0, 0), (8, 0), (8, 6) and (2, 9), taken in that order?
How many integers from 1 to 1000 are divisible by exactly one of 3, 5 and 7?
In how many distinct ways can the letters A, A, B, B, C, D be arranged in a row so that no two identical letters are next to each other?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Total arrangements = 6!/(2!2!) = 180. Arrangements with the two A's together: treat AA as one block: 5!/2! = 60; similarly 60 for BB. Both together: 4! = 24. Required = 180 − 60 − 60 + 24 = 84.

questions.question_text: Three fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum is even and at least one die shows a 6?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Even-sum outcomes: 108 of 216. Even-sum outcomes with no 6 use faces 1–5 (three odd, two even): all even = 2³ = 8, exactly two odd = 3 × 3² × 2 = 54, so 62 even-sum outcomes have no 6. Hence 108 − 62 = 46 favourable outcomes; probability 46/216 = 23/108.

questions.question_text: A trader buys 60 kg of rice. He sells one-third of it at a 20% profit and half of the remainder at a 10% loss. At what profit percentage must he sell the rest to make an overall profit of 12%?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Take CP = 1 per kg (total 60). 20 kg earn 24, 20 kg earn 18, so the last 20 kg must earn 67.2 − 42 = 25.2, a profit of 5.2/20 = 26%.

questions.question_text: Pipe A fills a tank in 12 hours and pipe B in 18 hours, while outlet C empties a full tank in 9 hours. All three are opened together on an empty tank and C is closed after 3 hours. How many hours in all does it take to fill the tank?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Rates: A + B − C = 1/12 + 1/18 − 1/9 = 1/36 per hour, so after 3 h the tank is 1/12 full. The remaining 11/12 at 1/12 + 1/18 = 5/36 per hour takes (11/12)(36/5) = 6.6 h. Total 3 + 6.6 = 9.6 hours.

questions.question_text: A sum doubles in 5 years at a certain rate of compound interest (compounded annually). In how many years will it become 16 times itself at the same rate?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Doubling every 5 years: 2 → 4 → 8 → 16 takes four doublings, 4 × 5 = 20 years.

questions.question_text: ₹7,800 is divided among P, Q and R so that 2 × (P's share) = 3 × (Q's share) = 4 × (R's share). What is Q's share, in ₹?
Four years ago, the average age of a family of 6 was 22 years. A child has been born since then, and today the average age of the 7 members is 22.5 years. How old is the child, in years?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Four years ago the six totalled 132; today they total 132 + 24 = 156. The seven total 7 × 22.5 = 157.5, so the child is 1.5 years old.

questions.question_text: How many integers n satisfy (n − 1)(n − 4)(n − 9)(n − 16) < 0 and 1 ≤ n ≤ 25?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The sign is negative between consecutive roots of alternating sign: 1 < n < 4 (n = 2, 3) and 9 < n < 16 (n = 10, …, 15). That gives 2 + 6 = 8 integers.

questions.question_text: For f(x) = (2x + 3)/(x − 1), x ≠ 1, what is f(f(f(2)))?
For real x, what is the minimum value of |x − 2| + |x − 5| + |x − 11|?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The sum of distances is minimised at the median, x = 5: 3 + 0 + 6 = 9.

questions.question_text: In triangle ABC, AB = 13, BC = 14 and CA = 15. What is the length of the altitude from A to BC?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: By Heron: s = 21, area = √(21 × 8 × 7 × 6) = 84. Altitude from A = 2 × 84/14 = 12.

questions.question_text: A square is inscribed in a semicircle of radius 5√5, with one side of the square on the diameter. What is the area of the square?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: With side s, the top corners are at (±s/2, s), so s²/4 + s² = 125, s² = 100.

questions.question_text: How many positive divisors of 10800 are perfect squares?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 10800 = 2⁴ × 3³ × 5². A square divisor uses even exponents: 2: {0, 2, 4} (3), 3: {0, 2} (2), 5: {0, 2} (2). Total 12.

questions.question_text: A committee of 5 is chosen from 6 men and 5 women so that it contains at least 2 women and at least 2 men. In how many ways can this be done?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Either 3 men + 2 women: 20 × 10 = 200, or 2 men + 3 women: 15 × 10 = 150. Total 350.

questions.question_text: Two numbers are chosen at random, without replacement, from {1, 2, …, 20}. What is the probability that their product is a multiple of 4?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Not a multiple of 4: both odd (C(10,2) = 45) or one odd and one ≡ 2 mod 4 (10 × 5 = 50). So 95 of 190 pairs fail, and the probability is 95/190 = 1/2.

questions.question_text: On a circular track of 1200 m, A and B start together from the same point in the same direction at 8 m/s and 5 m/s. After how many seconds do they meet for the first time at the starting point?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: A takes 150 s per lap and B 240 s, so both are at the start together after LCM(150, 240) = 1200 s.

questions.question_text: A shopkeeper marks every item 40% above cost. Cash buyers get a discount of d% on the marked price and card buyers get 2d%. In a month, the cost value of goods bought by card buyers was twice that bought by cash buyers, and his overall profit on cost was 12%. What is d?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Take cost 1 for cash sales and 2 for card sales (total 3). Revenue = 1.4(1 − d/100) + 2 × 1.4(1 − 2d/100) = 1.4(3 − 5d/100). Setting this equal to 3 × 1.12 = 3.36 gives 3 − 5d/100 = 2.4, so d = 12.

questions.question_text: P, Q and R can each finish a job alone in 20, 30 and 12 days respectively. They charge ₹1,500, ₹1,200 and ₹2,400 per day; a part-day is paid as a full day. Any of them may be hired on any day, and the job must be finished within 8 days. What is the minimum possible total wage bill, in ₹?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Step 1: cost of a whole job by each worker: P 20 × 1500 = 30,000, Q 30 × 1200 = 36,000, R 12 × 2400 = 28,800, so R is cheapest per unit of work, then P, then Q. Step 2: no one may work more than 8 days, so R does at most 8/12 = 2/3. Step 3: the remaining 1/3 is cheapest with P: 1/3 × 20 = 6.67, i.e. 7 paid days. But paying 7 full days wastes part of a day; compare R 8 + P 7 = 19,200 + 10,500 = 29,700 with R 7 + P 8 (7/12 + 8/20 = 0.983, not enough) and with R 8 + P 6 + Q 1 (2/3 + 0.3 + 1/30 = 1, cost 19,200 + 9,000 + 1,200 = 29,400). Step 4: checking all combinations, the minimum is ₹29,400.

questions.question_text: Solution A is 30% acid and solution B is 75% acid. In what ratio must A and B be mixed to get a 48% acid solution? Enter the ratio A : B as a single number A/B.
The ratio of boys to girls in a class is 7 : 5. After 8 boys leave and 4 girls join, the ratio becomes 1 : 1. How many students were originally in the class?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 7k − 8 = 5k + 4 gives k = 6, so the class had 12k = 72 students.

questions.question_text: The average of 11 consecutive odd numbers is 47. What is the product of the smallest and the largest of them?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The middle (6th) number is 47; the smallest is 47 − 10 = 37 and the largest 47 + 10 = 57. Product = 2109.

questions.question_text: For how many integers k with 1 ≤ k ≤ 30 does the equation x² + kx + 36 = 0 have two distinct real roots, both negative?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Both roots negative requires the sum −k < 0 (true for k ≥ 1) and product 36 > 0 (true). Distinct real roots need k² > 144, i.e. k ≥ 13. So k = 13, …, 30: 18 values.

questions.question_text: How many integers x satisfy |x − 3| + |x + 5| < 14?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: For −5 ≤ x ≤ 3 the sum is 8 < 14 (9 integers). For x > 3: 2x + 2 < 14 gives x < 6, i.e. 4, 5. For x < −5: −2x − 2 < 14 gives x > −8, i.e. −7, −6. Total 9 + 2 + 2 = 13.

questions.question_text: How many terms of the arithmetic progression 3, 7, 11, … are needed for the sum to exceed 2000 for the first time?
Real numbers x, y satisfy x + y = 7 and x³ + y³ = 133. What is x² + y²?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: x³ + y³ = (x + y)³ − 3xy(x + y): 133 = 343 − 21xy, so xy = 10. Then x² + y² = 49 − 20 = 29.

questions.question_text: In triangle PQR, the bisector of angle P meets QR at S. PQ = 12, PR = 18 and QR = 20. What is QS?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: By the angle bisector theorem, QS/SR = 12/18 = 2/3, so QS = 20 × 2/5 = 8.

questions.question_text: Two circles have radii 5 cm and 3 cm, and their centres are 17 cm apart. What is the length, in cm, of a transverse (internal) common tangent between the points of contact?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Transverse tangent length = √(d² − (r₁ + r₂)²) = √(289 − 64) = √225 = 15.

questions.question_text: A regular hexagon has side 6 cm. What is the area, in cm², of the triangle formed by joining three alternate vertices of the hexagon? Enter your answer as a multiple of √3 (e.g. 27 if the area is 27√3).
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Alternate vertices form an equilateral triangle of side 6√3, with area (√3/4) × 108 = 27√3.

questions.question_text: What is the sum of all positive divisors of 360 that are odd?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5. Odd divisors are divisors of 45: their sum is (1 + 3 + 9)(1 + 5) = 78.

questions.question_text: A bag has 5 red and 7 blue balls. Three balls are drawn at random without replacement. What is the probability that exactly two are red?

A trader uses a faulty balance. When buying, he receives 1100 g for every 1 kg he pays for; when selling, he gives only 900 g for every 1 kg he charges for. If he sells at his cost price per kg, what is his profit percentage?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: For ₹C he receives 1100 g. He sells it as 1100/900 = 11/9 'kg' at ₹C each, so revenue is 11C/9. Profit = 2/9 = 22 2/9 %.

questions.question_text: A can do a job in 20 days and B in 30 days. They work on alternate days, A starting. On which day is the job completed?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: In 2 days they do 1/20 + 1/30 = 1/12. After 22 days, 11/12 is done. On day 23 A does 1/20, making 11/12 + 1/20 = 58/60, still short. On day 24 B does 1/30, making 60/60. So the job is completed on day 24.

questions.question_text: A sum amounts to ₹13,310 in 3 years and to ₹14,641 in 4 years at compound interest (annual compounding). What is the sum, in ₹?
The cost of a diamond varies as the square of its weight. A diamond worth ₹1,60,000 breaks into three pieces whose weights are in the ratio 1 : 2 : 5. What is the loss, in ₹, due to the breakage?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Total 'square units': 8² = 64 before, 1 + 4 + 25 = 30 after. Loss = 160000 × 34/64 = ₹85,000.

questions.question_text: If x + 1/x = 3, what is the value of x⁵ + 1/x⁵?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Let tₙ = xⁿ + x⁻ⁿ, so tₙ₊₁ = 3tₙ − tₙ₋₁. t₀ = 2, t₁ = 3, t₂ = 7, t₃ = 18, t₄ = 47, t₅ = 123.

questions.question_text: How many ordered pairs of positive integers (x, y) satisfy 3x + 5y ≤ 60?
If log₂(log₃(log₄ x)) = 0, and y = log_x 2, what is 1/y?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: log₃(log₄ x) = 1, so log₄ x = 3 and x = 64. Then y = log₆₄ 2 = 1/6, so 1/y = 6.

questions.question_text: The sum of the first n terms of a sequence is 3n² + 5n. What is the sum of its 10th, 20th and 30th terms?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: aₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁ = 6n + 2. So a₁₀ + a₂₀ + a₃₀ = 62 + 122 + 182 = 366.

questions.question_text: Three numbers in a geometric progression have sum 26 and product 216. What is the largest of them?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Let the terms be a/r, a, ar. Then a³ = 216, so a = 6, and 6/r + 6 + 6r = 26 gives 3r² − 10r + 3 = 0, so r = 3 or 1/3. The terms are 2, 6, 18.

questions.question_text: ABCD is a square of side 12. E is the midpoint of BC and F lies on CD with CF = 3. What is the area of triangle AEF?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Area = square − ΔABE − ΔECF − ΔFDA = 144 − 36 − 9 − 54 = 45.

questions.question_text: What is the remainder when 7^99 is divided by 2400?
How many integers from 1 to 2000 are divisible by 6 or by 10, but not by 15?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Multiples of 6: 333; of 10: 200; of both (30): 66. Union = 467. A number in the union is divisible by 15 exactly when it is a multiple of 30 (6 and 15 give 30; 10 and 15 give 30): 66 of them. 467 − 66 = 401.

questions.question_text: In how many ways can the letters of the word BALLOON be arranged so that the two L's are not together?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Total = 7!/(2! 2!) = 1260. With the L's together (treat LL as one letter): 6!/2! = 360. So 1260 − 360 = 900.

questions.question_text: Two dice are rolled. Given that the sum is at least 9, what is the probability that at least one die shows 6?
The population of a town rises by 20% in the first year, falls by 25% in the second, and rises by 10% in the third. If it is 59,400 at the end of three years, what was the initial population?
A sells an article to B at a 20% profit; B sells it to C at a 10% loss; C sells it to D for ₹2,646, making a 22.5% profit. What did A pay for the article, in ₹?
A car covers the first third of a journey at 30 km/h, the second third at 45 km/h and the last third at 90 km/h. What is its average speed for the whole journey, in km/h?

Pipes A and B fill a tank in 12 and 15 hours; pipe C empties it in 20 hours. All three are opened together at 6 a.m., and C is closed at 10 a.m. At what hour of the day (in 24-hour format, e.g. 15 for 3 p.m.) is the tank full?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Net rate with C = 5/60 + 4/60 − 3/60 = 6/60 = 1/10, so 4 hours fill 2/5. The remaining 3/5 at 9/60 per hour takes 4 hours. The tank is full at 6 + 4 + 4 = 14, i.e. 2 p.m.

questions.question_text: The difference between compound interest and simple interest on a sum for 3 years at 10% per annum is ₹1,550. What is the sum, in ₹?
Let n be the least positive integer such that 180 divides 150ⁿ. If m is the least positive integer such that 150ⁿ divides 180ᵐ, what is m + n?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 180 = 2² × 3² × 5 and 150 = 2 × 3 × 5². Step 1: 150ⁿ = 2ⁿ3ⁿ5²ⁿ needs n ≥ 2 for both 2² and 3², so n = 2. Step 2: 150² = 2² × 3² × 5⁴ must divide 180ᵐ = 2²ᵐ3²ᵐ5ᵐ; the 5s force m ≥ 4, so m = 4. Step 3: m + n = 6.

questions.question_text: The roots of x² − 6x + k = 0 are α and β, with α² − β² = 24 and α > β. What is k?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: α + β = 6 and α² − β² = 24, so α − β = 4. Then α = 5, β = 1 and k = αβ = 5.

questions.question_text: If log₃ x + log₉ x + log₂₇ x = 11/2, what is x?
f(x) = (3x + 2)/(x − 3) for x ≠ 3. What is f(f(f(f(5))))?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: f(f(x)) = x for this function: (3f + 2)/(f − 3) = (3(3x+2) + 2(x−3))/((3x+2) − 3(x−3)) = 11x/11 = x. So applying f four times returns 5.

questions.question_text: In triangle ABC, AB = 13, BC = 14 and CA = 15. If m is the length of the median from A to BC, what is m²?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: By Apollonius' theorem, m² = (2b² + 2c² − a²)/4 = (450 + 338 − 196)/4 = 148.

questions.question_text: A ladder 25 m long leans against a vertical wall with its foot 7 m from the wall. If the top slides down 4 m, how far, in m, does the foot slide outward?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The original height is 24 m; the new height is 20 m. The new distance is √(625 − 400) = 15, so the foot slides 15 − 7 = 8 m.

questions.question_text: A rectangular sheet 44 cm × 18 cm is rolled along its longer side to form a hollow cylinder of height 18 cm. What is the volume of the cylinder, in cm³? (Take π = 22/7.)
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Circumference 44 = 2πr gives r = 7. Volume = (22/7) × 49 × 18 = 2772.

questions.question_text: What are the last two digits of 3^2026?
A bag holds 4 red and 6 blue balls. Balls are drawn one at a time, without replacement, until both colours have appeared. What is the expected number of draws?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Let D be the number of draws. D > k exactly when the first k balls are all one colour. Step 1: E[D] = Σₖ≥0 P(D > k) = 1 + Σₖ≥1 [P(first k all red) + P(first k all blue)]. Step 2: P(first k red) = C(4,k)/C(10,k) and P(first k blue) = C(6,k)/C(10,k). Step 3: red terms 4/10 + 6/45 + 4/120 + 1/210 = 0.5714…; blue terms 6/10 + 15/45 + 20/120 + 15/210 + 6/252 + 1/210 = 1.2. Step 4: E[D] = 1 + 0.5714… + 1.2 = 2.7714… = 97/35.

questions.question_text:
**Seminar week**

Six professors, A to F, each give one talk at a seminar running Monday to Saturday, one talk per day. Two talks are on Economics, two on History and two on Physics.

- B speaks on Thursday, on History.
- C speaks on the day immediately before E.
- A speaks on either Monday or Saturday, on Physics.
- F speaks on some day after D, and D does not speak on a day adjacent to B's.
- The two Economics talks are on consecutive days, but no two Physics talks are.
- C's talk is not on History. E speaks on Economics and F on Physics.

**Question:** Who speaks on Wednesday?

options.B: D
options.C: E

questions.pedagogical_explanation: B is on Thursday, so the C–E pair is Mon–Tue, Tue–Wed or Fri–Sat, and D can't be on Wed or Fri. If A is on Saturday: C–E on Mon–Tue leaves Wed and Fri for D and F (D can't take either). C–E on Tue–Wed gives D Mon, F Fri, but then A (Sat) and F (Fri) are consecutive Physics talks. So A is on Monday. C–E on Tue–Wed leaves Fri and Sat, with D forced to Sat and F after D, which is impossible. So C–E = Fri–Sat, D = Tue, F = Wed. Subjects: A, F Physics (Mon, Wed are not consecutive ✓). E (Sat) is Economics and the other Economics must be adjacent, so C (Fri). D (Tue) is History, as is B. Final: Mon A (Physics), Tue D (History), Wed F (Physics), Thu B (History), Fri C (Economics), Sat E (Economics).

questions.question_text:
**Seminar week**

Six professors, A to F, each give one talk at a seminar running Monday to Saturday, one talk per day. Two talks are on Economics, two on History and two on Physics.

- B speaks on Thursday, on History.
- C speaks on the day immediately before E.
- A speaks on either Monday or Saturday, on Physics.
- F speaks on some day after D, and D does not speak on a day adjacent to B's.
- The two Economics talks are on consecutive days, but no two Physics talks are.
- C's talk is not on History. E speaks on Economics and F on Physics.

**Question:** What is the subject of D's talk?

options.B: History
options.C: Physics

questions.pedagogical_explanation: B is on Thursday, so the C–E pair is Mon–Tue, Tue–Wed or Fri–Sat, and D can't be on Wed or Fri. If A is on Saturday: C–E on Mon–Tue leaves Wed and Fri for D and F (D can't take either). C–E on Tue–Wed gives D Mon, F Fri, but then A (Sat) and F (Fri) are consecutive Physics talks. So A is on Monday. C–E on Tue–Wed leaves Fri and Sat, with D forced to Sat and F after D, which is impossible. So C–E = Fri–Sat, D = Tue, F = Wed. Subjects: A, F Physics (Mon, Wed are not consecutive ✓). E (Sat) is Economics and the other Economics must be adjacent, so C (Fri). D (Tue) is History, as is B. Final: Mon A (Physics), Tue D (History), Wed F (Physics), Thu B (History), Fri C (Economics), Sat E (Economics). D speaks on Tuesday. The Physics talks are Mon and Wed and the Economics pair is Fri–Sat, so Tuesday is History.

questions.question_text:
**Seminar week**

Six professors, A to F, each give one talk at a seminar running Monday to Saturday, one talk per day. Two talks are on Economics, two on History and two on Physics.

- B speaks on Thursday, on History.
- C speaks on the day immediately before E.
- A speaks on either Monday or Saturday, on Physics.
- F speaks on some day after D, and D does not speak on a day adjacent to B's.
- The two Economics talks are on consecutive days, but no two Physics talks are.
- C's talk is not on History. E speaks on Economics and F on Physics.

**Question:** On which day is the second Physics talk of the week?

options.B: Wednesday
options.C: Friday

questions.pedagogical_explanation: B is on Thursday, so the C–E pair is Mon–Tue, Tue–Wed or Fri–Sat, and D can't be on Wed or Fri. If A is on Saturday: C–E on Mon–Tue leaves Wed and Fri for D and F (D can't take either). C–E on Tue–Wed gives D Mon, F Fri, but then A (Sat) and F (Fri) are consecutive Physics talks. Five teams A, B, C, D and E played a league in which every team played every other team exactly once. A win earned 3 points, a draw 1 point and a loss 0.

| Team | A | B | C | D | E |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Final points | 10 | 7 | 6 | 4 | 1 |

- A did not lose any match.
- B beat C.
- E's only point came from its match against A.

**Question:** What was the result of the match between B and D?

options.B: D won
options.C: Draw

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Each team plays 4 matches. A has 10 points and is unbeaten, so 3 wins + 1 draw, and the draw must be against E (E's only point). E lost the rest. **Bookshop sales (units)**

A bookshop's sales of four genres over three months are shown. Some entries are missing.

| Genre | Jan | Feb | Mar | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fiction | 40 | ? | ? | 150 |
| Science | ? | 20 | ? | 100 |
| History | 20 | ? | 30 | ? |
| Comics | ? | 30 | ? | 130 |
| Total | 150 | 140 | ? | 470 |

- Every entry in the table is a multiple of 10 between 10 and 90.
- In January, Comics sold exactly twice as many units as Science.

**Question:** Which genre had the highest total sales over the three months?

options.B: Science
options.C: History

questions.pedagogical_explanation: History total = 470 − 150 − 100 − 130 = 90 ⇒ History Feb = 40. Feb column: Fiction Feb = 140 − 20 − 40 − 30 = 50 ⇒ Fiction Mar = 60. January: Science + Comics = 150 − 40 − 20 = 90 with Comics = 2 × Science ⇒ Science Jan = 30, Comics Jan = 60. Then Science Mar = 50 and Comics Mar = 40. Totals: Fiction 150, Science 100, History 90, Comics 130.

questions.question_text:
**Coin game**

Asha and Bilal play a game with a pile of coins. They take turns, Asha first. On each turn a player must remove **1, 2 or 4** coins (never more than the pile holds). Under the standard rule, the player who takes the **last** coin wins. Both players always play perfectly.

**Question:** With 20 coins, how many coins must Asha remove on her first turn to be sure of winning?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Work backwards: a pile is 'losing' for the player to move if every move leads to a winning pile. 0 is losing. 1, 2 and 4 can reach 0, so they're winning. 3 → 2 or 1 only, so it's losing. In general, the losing piles are exactly the multiples of 3, because 1, 2 and 4 are never multiples of 3. 20 − 2 = 18 is a multiple of 3. Taking 1 (19) or 4 (16) leaves a winning pile for Bilal.

questions.question_text:
**Coin game**

Asha and Bilal play a game with a pile of coins. They take turns, Asha first. On each turn a player must remove **1, 2 or 4** coins (never more than the pile holds). Under the standard rule, the player who takes the **last** coin wins. Both players always play perfectly.

**Question:** Suppose players may remove 1, 2, 3 or 4 coins (last coin still wins). With 23 coins, how many should Asha remove first to be sure of winning?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: With moves 1–4, the losing piles are multiples of 5 (any move from 5k can be answered to return to 5(k − 1)). Asha should leave 20, so she takes 3.

questions.question_text:
**Coin game**

Asha and Bilal play a game with a pile of coins. They take turns, Asha first. On each turn a player must remove **1, 2 or 4** coins (never more than the pile holds). Under the standard rule, the player who takes the **last** coin wins. Both players always play perfectly.

**Question:** Now suppose the rule is reversed: the player who takes the last coin LOSES (moves are still 1, 2 or 4). With 10 coins, how many should Asha remove first to be sure of winning?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Now a pile of 1 is losing for the player to move, because they must take the last coin. Working upward: 2, 3 → can leave 1, so winning. 4 → leaves 3, 2 or 0, and 0 means you just took the last coin and lost, so 4 is losing. The losing piles are 1, 4, 7, 10, 13, … (one more than a multiple of 3). 10 is losing: from 10, Asha can leave 9, 8 or 6, and each lets Bilal move back to 7. So she cannot force a win.

questions.question_text:
**Sharing chocolates**

24 chocolates were shared among five friends P, Q, R, S and T. Each got at least one, and no two got the same number.

- Q got twice as many as R.
- S got exactly one more than T.
- P got as many as Q and T together, and P got the most.
- R got more than S.

**Question:** Who got the fewest chocolates?

options.B: R
options.C: S

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Let T = t, so S = t + 1. Let R = r, so Q = 2r and P = 2r + t. Total: (2r + t) + 2r + r + (t + 1) + t = 5r + 3t + 1 = 24 ⇒ 5r + 3t = 23. Options: (r, t) = (4, 1) or (1, 6). R > S rules out (1, 6) (R = 1 < S = 7). So P = 9, Q = 8, R = 4, S = 2, T = 1.

questions.question_text:
**Locker code**

A locker opens with a 4-digit code. All four digits are different and the first digit is not 0. Six guesses were tried, and each was given the feedback shown.

| Guess | Feedback |
|---|---|
| 7148 | 1 correct digit in the correct place |
| 2054 | 1 correct digit in the wrong place |
| 9361 | 1 correct digit in the correct place; 1 correct digit in the wrong place |
| 3520 | 2 correct digits in the wrong place |
| 8697 | 1 correct digit in the correct place; 1 correct digit in the wrong place |
| 1052 | 1 correct digit in the correct place |

**Question:** Which digit is in the second position of the code?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: (1) 2054 says exactly one of 2, 0, 5, 4 is in the code. 3520 says two of 3, 5, 2, 0 are, so 3 is in the code plus exactly one of 5, 2, 0, and 4 is out. (2) 9361 needs two of 9, 3, 6, 1, so one of 9, 6, 1 (call it y). 8697 needs two of 8, 6, 9, 7. If y = 1, there's no room for two of those, so y is 9 or 6 and the 4th digit (z) is 8 or 7. (3) 7148: exactly one digit, in place, so z sits where 7148 has it (7 → 1st place, 8 → 4th place). 1 is out. (4) 1052: one digit in place, so the digit x from {5, 2, 0} is where 1052 has it: 0 → 2nd, 5 → 3rd, 2 → 4th. But 2054 says x is misplaced there: 0 would be 2nd and 5 would be 3rd in both guesses, a contradiction. So x = 2 in 4th place, which forces z = 7 in 1st place. (5) The code is 7 _ _ 2 with 3 and y in the middle. 9361 needs exactly one in place: 7362 gives two in place and 7632 gives none, so y = 9. 7932 gives none in place, but 7392 gives 3 in place and 9 misplaced ✓. 8697 then gives 9 in place and 7 misplaced ✓. Code = 7392 (a computer check of all 4,536 possible codes confirms it's the only one).

**Four houses**

Kiran, Leela, Manav and Nisha live in four houses numbered 1 to 4 in a row. Each owns a different pet (cat, dog, parrot, fish) and drives a different coloured car (red, blue, white, black).

- Kiran and Nisha live in the two end houses.
- Leela owns the parrot. Kiran owns the fish.
- The fish lives in house 1, and the white car belongs to house 4.
- Manav drives the black car and does not own the cat.
- The red car belongs to the house immediately to the right of (one number higher than) the dog's house.

**Question:** Who owns the cat?

options.B: Leela
options.C: Manav

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Kiran owns the fish, which is in house 1, so Kiran = 1 and Nisha = 4 (white car). Leela and Manav are in houses 2 and 3. The dog isn't Kiran's, Leela's (parrot) or in house 4 (red must be to its right), so the dog is Manav's. Red is to the right of the dog and can't be house 4 (white), so Manav = 2 and red = 3 = Leela. Kiran drives blue and Nisha owns the cat.

questions.question_text:
**Three-round quiz**

Four contestants W, X, Y and Z played three rounds. In each round the contestants were ranked 1st to 4th (no ties) and earned 4, 3, 2 and 1 points respectively. The final totals were 10, 8, 7 and 5 points, in some order.

- Y had the highest total.
- X won Round 1 but came last in Round 3.
- Z came last in Round 1, and finished ahead of W in Round 2.
- Each round had a different winner.
- W's total was higher than Z's.

**Question:** Who won Round 3?

options.B: X
options.C: Y

questions.pedagogical_explanation: R1 winner is X and Z is last. Each round has a different winner, so Y wins exactly one of R2/R3. Y = 10 = 4 + 3 + 3, so Y is 2nd in the other two rounds, giving R1: X, Y, W, Z. X = 4 + (R2 points) + 1 must be 8, 7 or 5, so X is 2nd (X = 8) or 3rd (X = 7) in R2. Case Y wins R3: R2's winner is Z (Z must be ahead of W) and Y is 2nd, so X is 3rd (X = 7) and W 4th. Then W and Z must total 8 and 5. Z = 1 + 4 + (2 or 3) ≥ 7, so Z = 8 and W = 5, contradicting W > Z. So Y wins R2. If R2 = Y, Z, X, W, then X = 7, and R3 (won by W or Z) makes either W = 7 (a repeat of X's 7) or W < Z. So R2 = Y, X, Z, W and X = 8. R3 = winner, Y, other, X. Z winning gives Z = 7 > W = 5 ✗, so W wins. Final: R1 X > Y > W > Z; R2 Y > X > Z > W; R3 W > Y > Z > X. Totals W 7, X 8, Y 10, Z 5.

**Circular arrangement**

Seven musicians sit in a circle for a jam session, equally spaced and facing the centre. Each plays one instrument type — strings, percussion, wind — with three on strings and two each on the others. "Immediately to the left" is from the seated person's own point of view.

The following is known:

- Yash and Hina do not sit next to each other.
- Divya and Vani sit next to each other.
- Along the shorter way round, exactly two people sit between Yash and Bhavin.
- No two people with instrument type wind sit next to each other.
- Divya and Hina have the same instrument type.
- Vikram's instrument type is not wind.
- Divya and Jatin have the same instrument type.
- Yash and Vani have the same instrument type.
- Divya sits immediately to the left of Vikram.

**Question:** What is Divya's instrument type?

options.B: percussion
options.C: Cannot be determined

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Step 1: use "Divya sits immediately to the left of Vikram." — this fixes: Divya sits immediately to the left of Vikram. Step 2: use "Divya and Vani sit next to each other." — this fixes: Vani sits immediately to the left of Divya. Step 3: use "Along the shorter way round, exactly two people sit between Yash and Bhavin." — nothing is fixed outright yet, but it removes options needed later. Step 4: use "Divya and Hina have the same instrument type." — nothing is fixed outright yet, but it removes options needed later. Step 5: use "Divya and Jatin have the same instrument type." — this fixes: Divya's instrument type is strings; Hina's instrument type is strings; Jatin's instrument type is strings. Step 6: use "Vikram's instrument type is not wind." — this fixes: Vikram's instrument type is percussion. Step 7: use "Yash and Vani have the same instrument type." — this fixes: Yash's instrument type is wind; Bhavin's instrument type is percussion; Vani's instrument type is wind. Step 8: use "No two people with instrument type wind sit next to each other." — this fixes: Vikram sits immediately to the left of Yash; Bhavin sits immediately to the left of Vani. Step 9: use "Yash and Hina do not sit next to each other." — this fixes: Hina sits immediately to the left of Bhavin; Jatin sits immediately to the left of Hina; Yash sits immediately to the left of Jatin. Final arrangement: going round to each person's left starting from Vikram: Vikram (percussion), Divya (strings), Vani (wind), Bhavin (percussion), Hina (strings), Jatin (strings), Yash (wind). Reading off: strings.

questions.question_text:
Passage: For most of the twentieth century, a broken household object presented its owner with a simple calculation. A toaster, a radio or a pair of shoes was expensive relative to wages, while the labour needed to mend it was cheap. Repair shops lined the streets of every town, and the decision to fix rather than replace was so obvious that it hardly felt like a decision at all. Over the past few decades that arithmetic has quietly inverted. Manufacturing has become so efficient, and global supply chains so long, that a new appliance can cost less than an hour of a skilled technician's time. The repair shop has not been defeated by consumer laziness; it has been priced out.
Economists recognise this as a version of what is called the 'cost disease'. In sectors where productivity rises quickly, such as manufacturing, prices tend to fall; in sectors where it barely moves, such as hands-on services, wages must still keep pace with the rest of the economy, so prices rise. Repair belongs firmly to the second group. A technician diagnosing a faulty washing machine today works at roughly the same speed as one did fifty years ago, yet must be paid a modern wage. The relative price of fixing things therefore climbs year after year, regardless of anyone's intentions.
This framing matters because it changes what a sensible policy response looks like. If throwing things away were merely a cultural failing, the remedy would be exhortation: campaigns urging people to value what they own. But if the problem is mainly one of relative prices, moral appeals will achieve little. People respond to the costs in front of them, and most households cannot afford to pay more to keep an old machine running than to buy a new one, however virtuous that choice might be.
The more promising interventions therefore target the price gap directly. Some governments have experimented with lowering taxes on repair services, or with requiring manufacturers to sell spare parts and publish repair manuals for a set number of years. These right-to-repair rules are often described as consumer-protection measures, but their deeper effect is economic: by making parts available and designs easier to open, they reduce the hours a technician must spend on each job, and so attack the very cost that made repair uncompetitive.
None of this means that culture is irrelevant. Habits formed when repair was impractical can persist long after the economics improves, and a generation that has never had an object mended may not think to ask. But culture tends to follow prices more readily than it leads them. A society that wants its citizens to repair more would do better to make repair cheaper than to make them feel guilty.

The passage primarily argues that:

options.A: consumers today repair less than earlier generations because they value their possessions less
options.B: the decline of repair is driven mainly by shifting relative prices, so policy should narrow the cost gap rather than appeal to values
options.C: right-to-repair rules are essentially consumer-protection measures
options.D: manufacturing efficiency has made repair technicians less skilled over time

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage says repair 'has been priced out' (para 1), explains this through rising relative costs (para 2), and concludes that making repair cheaper beats making people feel guilty (paras 3–5). Option A is the view the author rejects ('not … consumer laziness'). Option C is described as how the rules are 'often described', and the author says their deeper effect is economic. Option D is never claimed: technicians work at the same speed, not with less skill.

Passage: Imagine two drivers who leave the same party, each having had a glass of wine too many. Both drive home along similar roads with the same degree of carelessness. On the first driver's route, nothing happens. On the second's, a child runs into the street, and the car cannot stop in time. Most of us judge the second driver far more harshly than the first; the law does too, imposing penalties of an entirely different order. Yet the two drivers did exactly the same thing. The only difference between them lies in something neither controlled: whether a child happened to step off the kerb.
Philosophers call this phenomenon moral luck, and the phrase is meant to sound uncomfortable. A widely shared intuition holds that we should be praised or blamed only for what is within our control. The careless drivers controlled how much they drank and whether they chose to drive, but not who crossed their path. If that intuition is right, then the two drivers deserve exactly the same blame, and our harsher verdict on the second is a kind of mistake.
The difficulty is that the control principle, applied consistently, threatens to swallow almost everything. We do not control the temperament we are born with, the upbringing that shaped our values, or the circumstances that test them. A person who would have collaborated with a tyrannical regime, had they lived under one, may live a blameless life simply because they were born elsewhere. If we strip away everything that luck has touched, it is not obvious that anything remains to be judged at all.
Some thinkers have responded by biting the bullet: moral assessment, they say, should attach only to the inner will, to intentions and choices, and outcomes are morally irrelevant. This view has the merit of consistency, but it struggles to explain experiences that seem central to moral life. The second driver will rightly feel something the first does not, a particular kind of regret that is more than mere sadness that a bad thing occurred. To tell him that his feelings rest on a confusion seems not merely unkind but false to what has happened.
Others argue that the right response is not to abolish moral luck but to accept it as a feature of our condition. On this view, we are not disembodied wills floating free of the world; we are agents whose actions spill into consequences we cannot fully foresee, and taking responsibility means owning those consequences, including the unlucky ones. The price of this acceptance is that morality becomes less tidy and, in a sense, less fair. But perhaps the demand that morality be perfectly fair was itself a fantasy, born of the hope that we could stand outside the world we act in.

The example of the two drivers is used mainly to:

options.A: show that drink-driving penalties are too lenient
options.B: illustrate a case in which our judgements of blame seem to depend on something outside the agents' control
options.C: argue that the second driver deserves no blame at all
options.D: demonstrate that intentions matter more than outcomes

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The paragraph ends: 'The only difference between them lies in something neither controlled', and the next paragraph names this 'moral luck'. The passage says nothing about the penalties being lenient (Option A). It never says the second driver is blameless (Option C). Option D is one view discussed later (the 'inner will' view), not the purpose of the example.

Passage: Imagine two drivers who leave the same party, each having had a glass of wine too many. Both drive home along similar roads with the same degree of carelessness. On the first driver's route, nothing happens. On the second's, a child runs into the street, and the car cannot stop in time. Most of us judge the second driver far more harshly than the first; the law does too, imposing penalties of an entirely different order. Yet the two drivers did exactly the same thing. The only difference between them lies in something neither controlled: whether a child happened to step off the kerb.
Philosophers call this phenomenon moral luck, and the phrase is meant to sound uncomfortable. A widely shared intuition holds that we should be praised or blamed only for what is within our control. The careless drivers controlled how much they drank and whether they chose to drive, but not who crossed their path. If that intuition is right, then the two drivers deserve exactly the same blame, and our harsher verdict on the second is a kind of mistake.
The difficulty is that the control principle, applied consistently, threatens to swallow almost everything. We do not control the temperament we are born with, the upbringing that shaped our values, or the circumstances that test them. A person who would have collaborated with a tyrannical regime, had they lived under one, may live a blameless life simply because they were born elsewhere. If we strip away everything that luck has touched, it is not obvious that anything remains to be judged at all.
Some thinkers have responded by biting the bullet: moral assessment, they say, should attach only to the inner will, to intentions and choices, and outcomes are morally irrelevant. This view has the merit of consistency, but it struggles to explain experiences that seem central to moral life. The second driver will rightly feel something the first does not, a particular kind of regret that is more than mere sadness that a bad thing occurred. To tell him that his feelings rest on a confusion seems not merely unkind but false to what has happened.
Others argue that the right response is not to abolish moral luck but to accept it as a feature of our condition. On this view, we are not disembodied wills floating free of the world; we are agents whose actions spill into consequences we cannot fully foresee, and taking responsibility means owning those consequences, including the unlucky ones. The price of this acceptance is that morality becomes less tidy and, in a sense, less fair. But perhaps the demand that morality be perfectly fair was itself a fantasy, born of the hope that we could stand outside the world we act in.

According to the passage, the main difficulty with applying the control principle consistently is that it:

options.A: would make the law too harsh on careless drivers
options.B: would leave little or nothing open to moral judgement, since so much that shapes us is beyond our control
options.C: cannot account for the intentions of agents
options.D: conflicts with the way courts assign penalties

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Paragraph 3: the principle 'threatens to swallow almost everything' (temperament, upbringing, circumstances), and 'it is not obvious that anything remains to be judged'. Option C is the reverse: the principle focuses on what we control, including intentions. Options 1 and 4 concern the law, which isn't the stated difficulty.

questions.question_text:
Passage: In the early 2010s, researchers in several fields began to confront an awkward possibility: that a substantial share of published findings might not hold up if the studies were simply run again. Large collaborative efforts set out to repeat well-known experiments in psychology, and later in economics and cancer biology, following the original methods as closely as possible. The results were sobering. In several of these projects, fewer than half of the repeated studies produced effects as strong as the originals, and some effects vanished altogether. The episode came to be known as the replication crisis.
It would be easy to read this as a story of fraud, but deliberate fabrication explains only a small part of it. The deeper causes are structural. Journals have long preferred to publish striking, positive results over null findings, and careers depend on publications. Under these pressures, researchers face many small decisions that seem individually harmless: which outliers to exclude, which of several measures to report, when to stop collecting data. Each choice can nudge a result across the conventional threshold of statistical significance. Taken together, such choices can make chance patterns look like real discoveries, even when no one intends to deceive.
The statistical threshold itself has come in for criticism. A result is conventionally called significant if, assuming there were no real effect, data at least as extreme would arise less than five per cent of the time. This is often misread as meaning that there is only a five per cent chance the finding is false. In reality, the probability that a significant result reflects a true effect depends heavily on how plausible the hypothesis was to begin with and on how much statistical power the study had. When many long-shot hypotheses are tested in small samples, a large fraction of the significant results can be false alarms.
Reformers have proposed a range of remedies. One of the most influential is preregistration, in which researchers publicly record their hypotheses and analysis plans before collecting data, so that later choices cannot be shaped by the results. Another is the registered report, a format in which a journal agrees to publish a study on the strength of its design, before the results are known, removing the incentive to produce a striking outcome. Larger samples, shared data and routine replication have also gained ground.
Some critics worry that these reforms may stifle exploratory research, the open-ended poking around that often precedes genuine breakthroughs. The reformers' usual reply is that exploration is welcome, provided it is labelled as such. The aim is not to forbid researchers from following hunches, but to stop hunches confirmed after the fact from being presented as predictions made in advance.

According to the passage, the replication crisis is mainly explained by:

options.B: publication incentives and many small analytical choices that can make chance patterns look like real findings
options.C: outdated laboratory equipment
options.D: journals refusing to publish psychology research

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Paragraph 2: 'deliberate fabrication explains only a small part', and 'the deeper causes are structural': journals preferring striking results, plus 'many small decisions' that can 'make chance patterns look like real discoveries'. Options 3 and 4 are never mentioned.

options.A: A significant result means there is at most a five per cent chance that the finding is false
options.B: Whether a significant result reflects a real effect depends partly on the hypothesis's prior plausibility and the study's statistical power
options.C: Significance thresholds played no role in the replication crisis
options.D: Testing many hypotheses in small samples makes false alarms rarer

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Paragraph 3 says this almost word for word. Option A is the misreading the passage warns against. Option C contradicts 'The statistical threshold itself has come in for criticism' and the role of nudging results 'across the conventional threshold'. Option D is the reverse of the final sentence of paragraph 3.

questions.question_text:
Passage: There is an old quip that poetry is what gets lost in translation. Like most quips, it contains a truth wrapped in an exaggeration. A poem is not simply a set of statements that could be restated in other words; it is a particular arrangement of sounds, rhythms and associations that belong to one language and no other. When a line in Urdu or Tamil depends on a word that means two things at once, or on a rhyme that exists only in that tongue, the translator faces a choice in which something must be given up.
Translators have broadly divided into two camps over how to make that sacrifice. The first holds that fidelity to meaning comes first: the translator's task is to carry across what the poem says, as precisely as possible, even if the result reads stiffly. The second argues that a poem which no longer works as a poem has not been translated at all, only paraphrased. For this camp, the translator must be willing to invent, to substitute a new rhyme or image that produces in the reader something like the effect the original produced in its first audience.
Each position has its characteristic failure. Strict fidelity can yield texts that are accurate in every particular and lifeless as a whole, like a pressed flower that preserves the shape of a bloom but none of its scent. Free recreation, on the other hand, risks replacing the original poet with the translator, so that readers praise a voice that was never really there. Some celebrated translations are admired precisely as poems in their own right, which is both a tribute to the translator and a quiet admission of distance from the source.
A third approach refuses to choose. Some translators publish the original alongside a literal version and a freer rendering, inviting readers to triangulate between them. Others add notes explaining the puns and allusions that could not survive the crossing. These methods ask more of the reader, but they treat the loss honestly rather than disguising it.
Perhaps the most useful way to see the problem is to abandon the idea that a translation could ever be a replacement for the original. A translation is better understood as a reading: one person's careful, partial and inevitably personal account of what a poem is and does. Seen this way, the existence of many competing translations is not a sign that the task has failed, but evidence of the poem's richness. Each version catches a different facet, and no single version, however skilled, can catch them all.

The author's central claim is that:

options.A: poetry cannot be translated in any meaningful sense
options.B: literal translations are always preferable to free ones
options.C: a translation is best seen as one partial reading rather than a replacement, so many translations reflect a poem's richness rather than failure
options.D: translators should always add explanatory notes

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The final paragraph states the author's conclusion: 'A translation is better understood as a reading', and many translations are 'evidence of the poem's richness'. Option A is called 'an exaggeration'. Option B ignores the failures of strict fidelity the author describes. Option D is only one method mentioned in paragraph 4, never a universal rule.
